Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › External Routes
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

External Routes & Redistribution

Understand ASBR roles, OSPF external metric types, and how to use Junos routing policies to export external routes safely.

In this lesson

Define ASBR. Compare E1 and E2 metrics. Configure redistribution using Junos routing policies and verify external LSAs and routes.

Why it matters

Proper redistribution prevents loops, ensures predictable path selection, and lets you shape exit points to external networks such as the internet.

Hands-on

Walk through a Junos policy example that redistributes a static route as E1 with a custom metric and verify on a downstream router.

Caution

Redistribution without filters or tags can create loops. Use precise route-filters and tags when redistributing bidirectionally.

Explore Key Topics
ASBR & Redistribution

How routers inject external routes into OSPF using Type 5/7 LSAs and the role of ASBRs.

E1 vs E2 Metrics

E2 uses a fixed external cost; E1 adds internal path cost to the ASBR. This changes preferred exit points.

Junos Policies

Use policy-statement rules to match routes, set metric, and apply export under protocols ospf for redistribution.

Visual Concept
ASBR
Connects OSPF to external domain
LSA Types
External networks appear as Type 5 LSAs (or Type 7 in NSSA). LSAs carry seed metric and metric type.
Verification
Use show ospf database external and show route protocol ospf to confirm redistributed networks.

screens.title: Autonomous System Boundary Router (ASBR)
screens.narratorSegment: An Autonomous System Boundary Router, or ASBR, is simply an OSPF router that connects the OSPF domain to an external routing domain and performs redistribution. Practically, an ASBR has at least one interface in an OSPF area and another that provides reachability to networks learned by a different protocol — for example BGP for internet prefixes, static routes for stub networks, or a legacy IGP. The ASBR's responsibility is to inject those external networks into the OSPF Link State Database as external LSAs so OSPF routers can learn them. In enterprise networks you typically place ASBRs at your edge where you have a stable path to the external domain. A common misconception is that any router with one external route is automatically an ASBR: the term implies active redistribution into OSPF, not merely having external interfaces. Example: R1 holds a static route to 172.16.0.0/24 and is configured to export that route into OSPF; R1 is functioning as an ASBR. Key operational checks are reachability to the external next-hop, correct routing-policy matches, and verification in the OSPF database for external LSAs. Think of the ASBR as the translator between routing worlds — it must be configured carefully to avoid advertising unintended routes.

keyIdea.text: An ASBR bridges OSPF and external domains by redistributing selected routes into the OSPF LSDB.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › ASBR
Definition

What an ASBR does

An ASBR redistributes routes learned from another routing domain into OSPF, generating external LSAs so OSPF routers learn those external prefixes.

Responsibility checklist
  • Has reachability to the external network
  • Matches routes with routing policy before redistribution
  • Sets metric and metric-type appropriately
  • Verifies external LSA advertisement
Concrete example
R1 holds static 172.16.0.0/24 next-hop 10.0.0.2 and exports it into OSPF using a routing policy; R1 acts as ASBR for that network.
Operational diagram
Layered cards show interfaces and flows:
External Domain
BGP, static next-hop, or legacy IGP
ASBR (Redistributor)
Matches route, sets metric/metric-type, exports to OSPF
OSPF Domain
Receives Type 5/7 LSAs, installs O E1/O E2 routes
Common misconception
Not every router with an external interface is an ASBR—only routers configured to redistribute those routes into OSPF are ASBRs.

screens.title: External LSAs: Type 5 and Type 7
screens.narratorSegment: When an ASBR redistributes an external prefix into OSPF, the information is encoded as an external LSA so OSPF routers can discover reachability. In standard OSPF areas external networks are advertised as Type 5 LSAs. In not-so-stubby areas, the ASBR originating the redistribution inside the NSSA produces Type 7 LSAs which a border area translator eventually converts to Type 5. The LSA carries the external network prefix, the seed metric provided by the ASBR, and the metric-type attribute that indicates E1 or E2 behavior. A useful mental model is to think of the LSA as a transport envelope: it declares the external destination and how OSPF should compare that route against other candidates. A concrete example: a static route redistributed by R1 will appear as a Type 5 external LSA with a seed metric. If the policy sets metric-type 1, receiving routers compute cost by adding internal cost to reach the ASBR. A frequent troubleshooting step is to run show ospf database external on the ASBR and neighbors to confirm the presence and attributes of the external LSA. Remember that LSA type indicates where the external route originates and how NSSA areas handle translation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › External LSAs
LSA types

Type 5 vs Type 7

Type 5 LSAs advertise external networks in standard OSPF areas. In NSSA areas redistributed routes appear as Type 7 and may be translated to Type 5 by an ABR.

LSA attributes to check
  • External prefix and mask
  • Seed metric value
  • Metric-type (E1 or E2)
  • Originating ASBR ID
Inspecting LSAs
Verification commands show the LSAs and their attributes. Use this information to confirm the seed metric and metric-type before trusting route selection across the domain.
Concrete verification
show ospf database external
Key takeaway
LSA type and attributes determine how OSPF distributes and compares external reachability.

screens.title: E2 Metric Behavior (External Type 2)
screens.narratorSegment: External Type 2 is the default OSPF metric for redistributed routes. The defining property of E2 is that OSPF uses only the external seed metric when comparing multiple advertisements of the same external prefix across different ASBRs. The internal cost to reach the ASBR is not included in the comparison. Concretely, imagine two ASBRs advertising the same external network: ASBR-A with external metric 10 and ASBR-B with external metric 5. Even if ASBR-B is further away inside the OSPF domain, the path via ASBR-B will be preferred because 5 is less than 10. A helpful analogy is a fixed price: the advertised external metric is like a sticker price; internal shipping distance does not change the sticker. This behavior leads to predictable selection when external metrics differ, but it can produce non‑optimal internal forwarding if the preferred ASBR is topologically distant. A common misconception is assuming internal path cost always matters — it does not for E2 comparisons. Use E2 when you want external policy to dominate selection and when exit cost should be controlled primarily by external metric values set at redistribution time.

keyIdea.title: E2 essence
keyIdea.text: E2 compares only the external seed metric; internal path cost to the ASBR is ignored when choosing between E2 paths.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › E2 Metrics
Behavior

External Type 2 (E2)

E2 routes compare only the external seed metric when multiple ASBRs advertise the same prefix. Internal cost to reach the ASBR is not part of the comparison.

Concrete example
ASBR-A advertises metric 10, ASBR-B advertises metric 5. OSPF chooses ASBR-B's path regardless of internal distance.
Misconception
Do not assume internal topology will influence E2 selection; only the external metric matters for comparison.
Decision aid
When to use E2
Use E2 when you want redistribution seed metrics to control exit selection irrespective of internal distances. It is simpler when exit cost should be externally determined.
Check your understanding
If two ASBRs advertise the same E2 network with different seed metrics, which wins? The lower seed metric wins regardless of internal cost.
Consider using E2 when you control external metrics centrally at redistribution points.
Key Takeaway
E2 equals fixed external cost comparison; internal path length does not change which ASBR is preferred.

screens.title: E1 Metric Behavior (External Type 1)
screens.narratorSegment: External Type 1 differs from E2 by adding the internal OSPF cost from the receiving router to the ASBR to the external seed metric. This makes the final cost behave closer to internal routes: the closer ASBR may become preferred even if its seed metric is larger. Imagine ASBR-A advertises the network with seed metric 10 but is one hop away; ASBR-B advertises with seed metric 5 but is many hops away. With E1, the receiving router adds the internal cost to each ASBR, which can make ASBR-A the preferred exit despite its higher seed metric. E1 is useful when you want shortest-path exit selection across multiple ASBRs, especially in multi-homed enterprise sites. A practical note: setting metric-type 1 in your routing policy ensures that OSPF path selection factors in local topology. A common mistake is setting E1 without considering seed metric ranges — choose seed metric values and internal costs so that final preferences reflect intended exit points. End with a reflective prompt: if you want traffic to leave via the nearest ASBR, E1 is the right choice; if you prefer centralized control by seed metrics, use E2.

keyIdea.title: E1 essence
keyIdea.text: E1 adds internal OSPF cost to the seed metric, enabling shortest-path exit selection to external networks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › E1 Metrics
Behavior

External Type 1 (E1)

With E1, OSPF computes cost by adding the external seed metric and the internal OSPF cost to reach the ASBR. This favors closer ASBRs when deciding an exit path.

Concrete scenario
ASBR-A seed 10, internal cost 1 => total 11. ASBR-B seed 5, internal cost 10 => total 15. E1 prefers ASBR-A because total 11<15.
When to choose E1
Use E1 for shortest-path exit
E1 is preferred when you want OSPF to pick the nearest ASBR rather than relying only on seed metrics.
Misconception
Do not assume E1 makes external paths appear as internal LSAs; they remain external LSAs but cost calculation includes internal distance.
Check your understanding
If your goal is proximity-based exit selection, configure metric-type 1 in the export policy for that redistributed route.

screens.title: Junos Routing Policy to Redistribute a Static Route
screens.narratorSegment: Junos OS uses policy-statement blocks to control redistribution. The pattern is simple: create a policy-statement that matches route protocol and prefix, set the metric and metric-type as needed, accept the route, and then apply the policy under protocols ospf with export. I will walk you through a canonical example used in labs. First, the policy matches static routes and the specific prefix 172.16.0.0/24. Then it sets metric 20 and metric-type 1 to make the route an E1 with a seed metric of 20. Finally, the policy is applied with set export REDISTRIBUTE-STATIC-TO-OSPF under edit protocols ospf. A common pitfall is forgetting to include the accept action or misplacing the policy under the wrong protocol stanza. Another is omitting metric-type, which leaves the route as E2 by default. Use the policy to tightly match only desired networks and avoid broad accepts that can flood OSPF with unintended external LSAs. After committing, verify using show ospf database external on the ASBR and show route protocol ospf on a neighbor to confirm the O E1 or O E2 designation. Junos Routing Policy to Redistribute a Static Route means create a policy matching exact routes, set metric and metric-type, and apply it with export under protocols ospf.. In practical terms, write a policy, set metric and metric-type, and apply export under ospf. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create a policy matching exact routes, set metric and metric-type, and apply it with export under protocols ospf.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Junos Policy
Configuration example
edit policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE-STATIC-TO-OSPF
set term 1 from protocol static
set term 1 from route-filter 172.16.0.0/24 exact
set term 1 then metric 20
set term 1 then metric-type 1
set term 1 then accept
commit

edit protocols ospf
set export REDISTRIBUTE-STATIC-TO-OSPF
commit
Explanation
  • Match the exact static prefix to avoid over-redistribution.
  • Set metric and metric-type before accept so OSPF uses E1 with the seed metric.
  • Apply policy under protocols ospf using export to push routes into OSPF LSDB.
Key Takeaway
Explicitly set metric-type and metric in the policy for predictable OSPF behavior.
Common mistake
Missing accept or a route-filter that is too broad leads to unexpected LSAs in OSPF.
Concrete scenario
R1: static 172.16.0.0/24 next-hop 10.0.0.2. Policy redistributes as E1 metric 20. R2 will show route as O E1 after verification.
Verification commands
show ospf database external
show route protocol ospf
detail 172.16.0.0/24

screens.title: Routing Policy Anatomy and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable redistribution policy follows a predictable structure: match precisely, set attributes, tag when needed, and accept. Start with a from clause that matches the exact protocol and prefix. For example, from protocol static and from route-filter 172.16.0.0/24 exact ensures you only touch the intended network. Next, set the attributes you need: metric for seed cost and metric-type to choose E1 or E2. If you may redistribute the route back into the original protocol later, add a route tag so you can identify and block it in reverse redistribution. Finally, include then accept. Order matters because attribute-setting actions should occur before accept. Best practices include using narrow route-filters, explicit metric values, and tags for bidirectional safety. Also comment and document the policy intent so future operators know why a redistribution exists. A common operational error is applying export in the wrong protocol stanza or forgetting that export pushes routes out of the local routing table into the protocol’s advertisement plane. Remember: precise match plus explicit attributes prevents accidental advertisement of internal-only networks. Routing Policy Anatomy and Best Practices means match narrowly, set explicit metrics and types, tag if needed, and only accept intended networks to avoid wide redistribution.. In practical terms, match, set attributes, tag, and accept — a safe redistribution workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Policy Anatomy
Four step workflow
1. Match precisely
Use protocol and route-filter exact matches to avoid over-broad accepts.
2. Set attributes
Set metric and metric-type before accepting so OSPF sees the values on distribution.
3. Tag when needed
Apply route tags to prevent loops if redistribution occurs both directions between protocols.
4. Accept
Finally, accept the route so it is exported into OSPF.
Pro tip
Document why each redistribution exists and keep policies as small as possible.
Warning
Don't accept everything: broad accepts create many external LSAs and possible loops.
Example policy snippet
set term 1 from protocol static
set term 1 from route-filter 172.16.0.0/24 exact
set term 1 then metric 50
set term 1 then metric-type 1

Why tag?
Tags let you filter the same route when importing from OSPF back into the external protocol to prevent re-advertisement loops.

screens.title: Applying Export vs Import — Which Direction Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Junos distinguishes export and import policies to control what a routing protocol advertises and what it accepts into the local routing table. For redistributing into OSPF we use export under protocols ospf because we are moving routes from the routing table into OSPF advertisements. Import policies apply when learning routes from a protocol into the local routing table. Confusing these two is a frequent operational error. For example, creating a policy but adding it under import in protocols ospf will not cause the static route to be advertised into OSPF. Another mistake is applying the export policy to the wrong protocol — for example applying it under protocols bgp instead of ospf when the intention is to announce into OSPF. To avoid this, document the intent in the policy name and include a single comment line at the top of the policy to indicate direction. Always verify the exported route appears in show ospf database external and that remote routers list it as O E1 or O E2 in show route protocol ospf. This check confirms the export worked and that the route attributes are as expected.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: Redistribution mistakes are predictable and fixable if you follow a short checklist. First, missing or incorrect policy: ensure the policy exists, matches the intended routes, and has then accept. Use show configuration policy-options policy-statement to inspect the policy. Second, wrong export/import usage: remember that export under protocols ospf controls what is advertised; import is for learning from a protocol. Third, routing loops from bidirectional redistribution: prevent this by tagging redistributed routes and filtering tags when re-importing into the original protocol. Fourth, metric mismatches and unintended preferences: explicitly set metric-type and metric values to avoid relying on defaults. Fifth, ASBR reachability: the ASBR must have a working path to the external next-hop — otherwise the static route may not exist in the routing table to be redistributed. For each problem, the fix is direct: correct the policy match, apply the policy in the correct protocol stanza, add tags and filters, set explicit metrics, and confirm next-hop reachability. Use the verification commands after each change to ensure the network reflects your intent. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore how OSPF connects to networks outside the OSPF domain. You will learn what an Autonomous System Boundary Router is, why redistribution is necessary in real enterprise networks, and how Junos routing policies let you control which external routes are advertised and how they appear to OSPF routers. Redistribution is not a mystery — it is simply taking a route learned by another mechanism and representing it inside OSPF using external LSAs. We will compare the two OSPF external metric types, E2 and E1, with concrete examples so you can predict path selection when multiple ASBRs advertise the same network. You will also follow a Junos configuration pattern: build a routing policy that matches a static route, set the metric and metric-type, and apply that policy with an export statement under protocols ospf. Finally, we cover verification commands and the common mistakes that cause loops or unexpected routes. By the end you will be able to plan redistribution safely and verify its results in the OSPF database and routing tables.

These objectives map to hands-on skills and conceptual understanding you will build during the lesson. First, you will be able to explain the role of an Autonomous System Boundary Router in connecting OSPF to other routing domains, describing why an ASBR is necessary and how it advertises external networks using external LSAs. Second, you will learn to differentiate the two OSPF external metric types, E2 and E1, including how E2 treats the external seed metric as the primary comparator while E1 adds the internal cost to reach the ASBR. Third, you will configure redistribution from static or other protocol-sourced routes into OSPF on Junos OS by writing a routing policy that matches the desired route. Fourth, you will apply that routing policy under protocols ospf with the export statement so OSPF advertises the matched routes. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you have achieved it.

The second objectives set focuses on operational control and safety. First, you will learn to use routing policy primitives to set metric-type and metric values during redistribution, controlling whether a route behaves like E1 or E2 in OSPF. Second, you will understand the verification commands to inspect the OSPF database for external LSAs and to read routing table entries that indicate O E1 or O E2. Third, you'll study common mistakes that cause redistribution problems — for example, missing route-filters, applying export versus import incorrectly, and not tagging routes when redistributing bidirectionally. Fourth, you will develop troubleshooting steps such as checking the policy match, ensuring the ASBR has reachability to the external network, and confirming the applied export under protocols ospf. Each objective ties to measurable checks so you can validate correct behavior in a lab or production environment.

An Autonomous System Boundary Router, or ASBR, is simply an OSPF router that connects the OSPF domain to an external routing domain and performs redistribution. Practically, an ASBR has at least one interface in an OSPF area and another that provides reachability to networks learned by a different protocol — for example BGP for internet prefixes, static routes for stub networks, or a legacy IGP. The ASBR's responsibility is to inject those external networks into the OSPF Link State Database as external LSAs so OSPF routers can learn them. In enterprise networks you typically place ASBRs at your edge where you have a stable path to the external domain. A common misconception is that any router with one external route is automatically an ASBR: the term implies active redistribution into OSPF, not merely having external interfaces. Example: R1 holds a static route to 172.16.0.0/24 and is configured to export that route into OSPF; R1 is functioning as an ASBR. Key operational checks are reachability to the external next-hop, correct routing-policy matches, and verification in the OSPF database for external LSAs. Think of the ASBR as the translator between routing worlds — it must be configured carefully to avoid advertising unintended routes.

When an ASBR redistributes an external prefix into OSPF, the information is encoded as an external LSA so OSPF routers can discover reachability. In standard OSPF areas external networks are advertised as Type 5 LSAs. In not-so-stubby areas, the ASBR originating the redistribution inside the NSSA produces Type 7 LSAs which a border area translator eventually converts to Type 5. The LSA carries the external network prefix, the seed metric provided by the ASBR, and the metric-type attribute that indicates E1 or E2 behavior. A useful mental model is to think of the LSA as a transport envelope: it declares the external destination and how OSPF should compare that route against other candidates. A concrete example: a static route redistributed by R1 will appear as a Type 5 external LSA with a seed metric. If the policy sets metric-type 1, receiving routers compute cost by adding internal cost to reach the ASBR. A frequent troubleshooting step is to run show ospf database external on the ASBR and neighbors to confirm the presence and attributes of the external LSA. Remember that LSA type indicates where the external route originates and how NSSA areas handle translation.

External Type 2 is the default OSPF metric for redistributed routes. The defining property of E2 is that OSPF uses only the external seed metric when comparing multiple advertisements of the same external prefix across different ASBRs. The internal cost to reach the ASBR is not included in the comparison. Concretely, imagine two ASBRs advertising the same external network: ASBR-A with external metric 10 and ASBR-B with external metric 5. Even if ASBR-B is further away inside the OSPF domain, the path via ASBR-B will be preferred because 5 is less than 10. A helpful analogy is a fixed price: the advertised external metric is like a sticker price; internal shipping distance does not change the sticker. This behavior leads to predictable selection when external metrics differ, but it can produce non‑optimal internal forwarding if the preferred ASBR is topologically distant. A common misconception is assuming internal path cost always matters — it does not for E2 comparisons. Use E2 when you want external policy to dominate selection and when exit cost should be controlled primarily by external metric values set at redistribution time.

External Type 1 differs from E2 by adding the internal OSPF cost from the receiving router to the ASBR to the external seed metric. This makes the final cost behave closer to internal routes: the closer ASBR may become preferred even if its seed metric is larger. Imagine ASBR-A advertises the network with seed metric 10 but is one hop away; ASBR-B advertises with seed metric 5 but is many hops away. With E1, the receiving router adds the internal cost to each ASBR, which can make ASBR-A the preferred exit despite its higher seed metric. E1 is useful when you want shortest-path exit selection across multiple ASBRs, especially in multi-homed enterprise sites. A practical note: setting metric-type 1 in your routing policy ensures that OSPF path selection factors in local topology. A common mistake is setting E1 without considering seed metric ranges — choose seed metric values and internal costs so that final preferences reflect intended exit points. End with a reflective prompt: if you want traffic to leave via the nearest ASBR, E1 is the right choice; if you prefer centralized control by seed metrics, use E2.

Junos OS uses policy-statement blocks to control redistribution. The pattern is simple: create a policy-statement that matches route protocol and prefix, set the metric and metric-type as needed, accept the route, and then apply the policy under protocols ospf with export. I will walk you through a canonical example used in labs. First, the policy matches static routes and the specific prefix 172.16.0.0/24. Then it sets metric 20 and metric-type 1 to make the route an E1 with a seed metric of 20. Finally, the policy is applied with set export REDISTRIBUTE-STATIC-TO-OSPF under edit protocols ospf. A common pitfall is forgetting to include the accept action or misplacing the policy under the wrong protocol stanza. Another is omitting metric-type, which leaves the route as E2 by default. Use the policy to tightly match only desired networks and avoid broad accepts that can flood OSPF with unintended external LSAs. After committing, verify using show ospf database external on the ASBR and show route protocol ospf on a neighbor to confirm the O E1 or O E2 designation. Junos Routing Policy to Redistribute a Static Route means create a policy matching exact routes, set metric and metric-type, and apply it with export under protocols ospf.. In practical terms, write a policy, set metric and metric-type, and apply export under ospf. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A reliable redistribution policy follows a predictable structure: match precisely, set attributes, tag when needed, and accept. Start with a from clause that matches the exact protocol and prefix. For example, from protocol static and from route-filter 172.16.0.0/24 exact ensures you only touch the intended network. Next, set the attributes you need: metric for seed cost and metric-type to choose E1 or E2. If you may redistribute the route back into the original protocol later, add a route tag so you can identify and block it in reverse redistribution. Finally, include then accept. Order matters because attribute-setting actions should occur before accept. Best practices include using narrow route-filters, explicit metric values, and tags for bidirectional safety. Also comment and document the policy intent so future operators know why a redistribution exists. A common operational error is applying export in the wrong protocol stanza or forgetting that export pushes routes out of the local routing table into the protocol’s advertisement plane. Remember: precise match plus explicit attributes prevents accidental advertisement of internal-only networks. Junos distinguishes export and import policies to control what a routing protocol advertises and what it accepts into the local routing table. For redistributing into OSPF we use export under protocols ospf because we are moving routes from the routing table into OSPF advertisements. Import policies apply when learning routes from a protocol into the local routing table. Confusing these two is a frequent operational error. For example, creating a policy but adding it under import in protocols ospf will not cause the static route to be advertised into OSPF. Another mistake is applying the export policy to the wrong protocol — for example applying it under protocols bgp instead of ospf when the intention is to announce into OSPF. To avoid this, document the intent in the policy name and include a single comment line at the top of the policy to indicate direction. Always verify the exported route appears in show ospf database external and that remote routers list it as O E1 or O E2 in show route protocol ospf. This check confirms the export worked and that the route attributes are as expected.

Redistribution mistakes are predictable and fixable if you follow a short checklist. First, missing or incorrect policy: ensure the policy exists, matches the intended routes, and has then accept. Use show configuration policy-options policy-statement to inspect the policy. Second, wrong export/import usage: remember that export under protocols ospf controls what is advertised; import is for learning from a protocol. Third, routing loops from bidirectional redistribution: prevent this by tagging redistributed routes and filtering tags when re-importing into the original protocol. Fourth, metric mismatches and unintended preferences: explicitly set metric-type and metric values to avoid relying on defaults. Fifth, ASBR reachability: the ASBR must have a working path to the external next-hop — otherwise the static route may not exist in the routing table to be redistributed. For each problem, the fix is direct: correct the policy match, apply the policy in the correct protocol stanza, add tags and filters, set explicit metrics, and confirm next-hop reachability. Use the verification commands after each change to ensure the network reflects your intent. These three core ideas summarize the chapter. First, an ASBR is the router that connects OSPF to another routing domain and is responsible for redistributing selected routes into OSPF. Second, redistribution injects external prefixes into the OSPF LSDB using external LSAs; confirm these LSAs with appropriate show commands. Third, routing policies in Junos are the control point: match precisely, set metric and metric-type, tag when necessary, then export. Together these points form the operational foundation for safe redistribution and predictable path selection. Keep these concepts top of mind when designing edge routing and when troubleshooting unexpected external routes in an OSPF domain.
